title: Short Stuff: Adam's Apples and Throat Lumps
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Adam's apple and the lump in the throat. Josh and Chuck open by noting the prominent laryngeal prominence, and dismiss the Biblical forbidden-apple folklore: the Adam's apple is the larynx (voice box) cartilage growing during male puberty under testosterone, which deepens the voice. Women have smaller larynxes and higher voices but can also have a visible Adam's apple. They discuss the tracheal shave (feminizing laryngoplasty) as a procedure that changes appearance but not voice, and that voice-feminizing surgery alters vocal cord length instead. The second half covers the lump-in-the-throat sensation (globus sensation): stress triggers fight-or-flight, which opens the glottis to take in more oxygen, while trying to hold back tears means holding breath or swallowing, so the glottis is pulled both open and closed, producing the sensation.

segments.title: Opening banter and Adam's apple introduction
segments.summary: Josh and Chuck joke about their own small Adam's apples and introduce the topic, citing a HowStuffWorks-linked article.

segments.title: What the Adam's apple really is
segments.summary: The Biblical forbidden-apple folklore is dismissed. The Adam's apple is the larynx cartilage growing during puberty under testosterone, which deepens the voice. Women have smaller larynxes and higher voices, and a prominent Adam's apple can appear in women too.

segments.title: Tracheal shave and voice feminization surgery
segments.summary: A tracheal shave (feminizing laryngoplasty) reduces a prominent Adam's apple and is discussed as a safe option for women and trans women, but it does not change the voice. Voice-feminizing surgery alters vocal cord length instead.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Hosts take a break before the next topic.

segments.title: Lump in the throat and the globus sensation
segments.summary: The lump-in-the-throat feeling (globus sensation) is explained: stress triggers fight-or-flight, which opens the glottis, while holding back tears involves holding breath or swallowing, so the glottis is pulled open and closed at once.

segments.summary: Hosts agree the episode is complete and close the show with a note about iHeartRadio podcasts.
